figure.name: John Locke
figure.role: Philosopher of property, liberal rights, toleration, and government by consent.
figure.hook: Locke = property rights + consent of government.
whyHere: Locke belongs here because he helps establish the liberal argument for natural rights, private property, consent of government, toleration, and resistance to tyranny.

That matters because later capitalism uses this language to defend property and markets, while socialism later asks whether property rights protect everyone equally, or protect owners more than workers.
figure.cleanIdea: If people have natural rights, including property, then government exists to protect those rights, and loses legitimacy when it violates them.

figure.discussionText: This is the planned debate room for Locke: property, consent, toleration, natural rights, and the socialist challenge that comes later.

ideas.title: Property
ideas.plainDefinition: Property means the things people can claim as theirs, use, protect, transfer, or exclude others from using.
ideas.context: In the Locke path, property is not just "stuff I own." It connects labor, liberty, personhood, and limits on government.
ideas.whyMatters: Locke makes property part of the liberal freedom argument: if people have natural rights, government should protect property instead of treating all land, labor, and wealth as the ruler's prize. The socialist question arrives later: what happens when property rights protect owners more strongly than workers?

ideas.title: Liberalism
ideas.plainDefinition: Liberalism is a political tradition built around rights, law, consent, toleration, and limits on arbitrary power.
ideas.context: Hot2Trotski uses Locke to show one early liberal foundation that socialism later argues with, not to turn Locke into the whole story of capitalism.
ideas.whyMatters: Locke gives the road a rights-and-limits vocabulary: people are not born to obey kings automatically, and government has to answer to rights, law, and consent. That vocabulary becomes part of the liberal defense of markets and property, then becomes something socialist critics test against industrial inequality.

ideas.title: Consent
ideas.plainDefinition: Consent means political authority is legitimate because people agree to it, not because rulers automatically own obedience.
ideas.context: This is the anti-divine-right door into the modern political road.
ideas.whyMatters: Locke ties government to consent so power has a test: it must protect the people and their rights. If government violates that trust, it loses legitimacy. That idea matters later because democratic movements, liberal reformers, and socialist organizers all argue over who really counts in that consent.

ideas.title: Natural Rights
ideas.plainDefinition: Natural rights are rights people are treated as having before government grants permission.
ideas.context: In the Locke path, life, liberty, property, conscience, and resistance to tyranny become part of the ground government must answer to.
ideas.whyMatters: Natural rights are the reason Locke can put limits on government. If rights come before the state, then the state is not the source of all political truth. Later arguments about capitalism and socialism keep returning to this pressure point: which rights are protected, and whose freedom becomes real in daily life?
